0.name: block
0.value:
Gives the variance of an array: the average of the squared distances of its values from their mean.

The variance is the standard deviation squared. It carries the same information as np.std - how spread out the values are - but in squared units, so it grows much faster: double the spread and the variance goes up four times. Reach for it where the maths wants it: variances of independent noises add (stds do not), so combining or comparing noise levels, weighting by 1 / variance, or fitting is done in variance. For a number to read or a threshold to set, np.std, in the data's own units, is usually easier.

HOW IT IS WORKED OUT:
Take the mean; take each value's distance from it; square the distances and average them. It divides by the number of values N (the "population" variance); some tools divide by N - 1, which gives a larger answer for small arrays: for 1 2 3 4 np.var gives 1.25, a spreadsheet's VAR 1.667.

THE axis MENU:
With no axis (the default) the whole array is reduced to one number. With axis 0 the reduction runs DOWN each column, giving one result per column; with axis 1 it runs ALONG each row, giving one result per row. For a table of 5 frames (rows) of 4 sensors (columns), axis 0 answers "what did each sensor read on average", axis 1 "what did all the sensors read on average at each frame". The axis named is the one that disappears: a 5 by 4 array gives 4 values on axis 0, 5 on axis 1.

SYNTAX:
np.var <axis: int>
With no argument there is no axis: one variance for the whole array.

EXAMPLE:
np.var

INPUTS and PARAMETERS:

in:
The array (a list or a single number is turned into one). Every array that arrives is measured and the result sent - the only inlet that makes the node send.

axis (menu, also an inlet):
Which way to reduce - see THE axis MENU. Changing it does NOT send by itself; the next array uses it. The menu offers None (the whole array) and the axes the last array had (None and 0 for a 1-D array); a message None into the axis inlet also returns to the whole array. An axis the array does not have is treated as its last axis for that array only: the choice is kept, so one 1-D array through np.var 1 does not stop the 2-D arrays that follow from being averaged along axis 1.

OUTPUTS:

var:
With no axis, one number, never negative. With an axis, an array one dimension smaller: one variance per column (axis 0) or per row (axis 1).

THE DEMO:
make_noise makes 64 random values, scaled so that at spread 1 and shift 0 their mean is exactly 0 and their standard deviation exactly 1. The spread slider multiplies them all; the shift slider adds to them all. The plot shows the 64 values as points.

READING THE DEMO:
np.var and np.std watch the same 64 values. Drag spread to 2: the std reads 2 and the variance 4. Spread 3: std 3, variance 9. The std through pow 2 (squared) reads the same as np.var, always. Below spread 1 the variance is the SMALLER of the two (0.5 squared is 0.25). Drag shift and neither moves - moving all the values together does not spread them.

RELATED:
np.std is the square root of the variance, in the data's own units. np.mean is the centre the distances are measured from. pow raises a number to a power - pow 2 squares, pow 0.5 takes the square root, which turns a variance back into a std.
